paragraphs.text: 1. "Do you," you say, "bid me avoid the crowd, withdraw, and be content with my own conscience? Where are those precepts of your school, which command us to die in action?" As for that—that I seem to you for the present to be counselling inaction—it is for this that I have shut myself away and barred the doors, that I might be able to help the greater number. No day passes for me in idleness. I claim part of the nights for my studies. I do not give myself to sleep, but yield to it, and hold my eyes, wearied and sinking with watching, to their task.

2. I have withdrawn not only from men, but from affairs, and chiefly from my own affairs; I am doing the business of posterity. For them I write down some things that may be of use. Wholesome admonitions, like the prescriptions of useful medicines, I commit to writing, having found them effective upon my own sores, which, even if they are not wholly healed, have at least ceased to spread.

3. The straight road, which I came to know late and wearied with wandering, I point out to others. I cry aloud: "Avoid whatever pleases the crowd, whatever chance has bestowed. Halt suspicious and trembling before every fortuitous good; both wild beast and fish are caught by some enticing hope. Do you think these the gifts of Fortune? They are snares. Whoever of you would lead a safe life, let him as far as ever he can shun these limed benefits, in which we too, most wretched of all, are deceived: we think we possess them, when we are caught fast.

4. That course leads down into the abyss. The end of this lofty life is to fall. Then it is not even permitted to make a stand, once prosperity has begun to drive us sidelong; or it must, if not in a straight line, at least overturn us at one blow. Fortune does not overthrow; she dashes headlong and impales."

5. Hold fast, then, to this sound and wholesome rule of life: indulge the body only so far as is enough for good health. It must be treated rather harshly, lest it obey the mind ill. Let food appease hunger, drink quench thirst, clothing keep off the cold, the house be a defence against what assails the body. Whether walls have been raised by turf or by the varied stone of a foreign people makes no difference; know that a man is sheltered just as well by thatch as by gold. Despise all those things that superfluous labour sets up as ornament and adornment. Reflect that nothing is to be wondered at except the mind, to which, being great, nothing is great.

6. If I speak thus with myself, if I speak thus with posterity, do I not seem to you to be of more use than when I used to go down as advocate to a court appearance, or set my seal upon the tablets of a will, or lend my voice and hand in the Senate to a candidate? Believe me, those who seem to do nothing are doing greater things; they are handling things human and divine together.

7. But now an end must be made, and, as I have established, something must be paid out for this letter. It shall not be done out of my own purse; I am still rifling Epicurus, whose saying I read this very day: "You must be a slave to philosophy, that true freedom may fall to your lot." He who has submitted and given himself over to her finds his cause not put off from day to day; he is set free at once. For this very thing, to be a slave to philosophy, is freedom.

8. It may be that you will ask me why I quote so many fine sayings from Epicurus rather than from our own school. But why should you suppose these to be Epicurus's words, and not common property? How many poets say things that have been said, or ought to be said, by philosophers! I will not touch the tragedians, nor our own toga-clad plays; for these too have something of seriousness, and stand midway between comedies and tragedies. How many most eloquent verses lie buried among the mimes! How many lines of Publilius ought to be spoken not by actors in slippers, but by actors in the buskin!

9. One verse of his that bears upon philosophy and upon this very part that was just now in our hands, I will quote—the verse in which he denies that what is fortuitous should be reckoned our own: "Whatever comes by our wishing is another's."

10. This thought you yourself put better, in fewer words: "What Fortune has made yours is not your own." And this, still better said by you, I will not pass over: "The good that could be given can be taken away." I do not charge this to the account as repayment; I have given you what was your own. Farewell.

1. What you ask about is one of those things which it concerns one to know only for the sake of knowing. But none the less, because it does concern you, you are in haste and unwilling to wait for the books which at this very moment I am arranging, containing the whole moral part of philosophy. I will dispatch it at once; yet I will first write how this craving for learning, with which I see you burning, should be ordered, lest it impede its own self.

2. We must neither pluck at things here and there, nor greedily fall upon them all at once; the whole is reached by parts. The load must be fitted to one's strength, nor must we take up more than we can be equal to. Not as much as you wish, but as much as you can hold, must be drawn off. Only keep a good heart; you will hold as much as you wish. The more the mind takes in, the more it expands itself.

3. I remember that Attalus used to give us this precept, when we besieged his school and came first and went out last, and even drew him into some discussions as he walked, for he was not only ready for learners but went to meet them. "The same purpose," he said, "ought to belong both to the teacher and to the learner: that the one wish to do good, the other to make progress."

4. He who comes to a philosopher should carry away with him something good each day: let him return home either sounder, or more curable. And he will return so; such is the power of philosophy that it helps not only those who study it, but even those who associate with it. He who has come into the sun, though he came not for this, will be tanned; those who have sat in a perfumer's shop and lingered a little longer carry away with them the scent of the place. And those who have been with a philosopher must needs have drawn off something to profit even the careless. Mark what I say: the careless, not the resisting.

5. What then? Do we not know some who have sat for many years with a philosopher and have not even taken a tinge of colour? Why should I not know them? Most persistent indeed and assiduous men, whom I call not the disciples of philosophers, but their lodgers.

6. Some come to hear, not to learn, just as we are drawn to the theatre for pleasure, to charm the ears with a speech or a voice or a play. You will see a great part of the audience to whom the philosopher's school is a lounging-place of leisure. They do not aim to lay aside any of their vices there, to receive any rule of life by which to test their conduct, but to enjoy a delight of the ears. Some, however, come even with note-tablets, not to catch the matter, but the words, which they utter with as little profit to others as they hear them without profit to themselves.

7. Some are roused by magnificent utterances and pass over into the feeling of the speakers, alert in face and mind, and are stirred no otherwise than eunuchs are wont to be by the sound of the Phrygian flute, raving at command. The beauty of things sweeps them along and goads them, not the sound of empty words. If anything is said keenly against death, anything defiantly against fortune, it delights us at once to put into practice what we hear. They are affected by these things and are such as they are bidden to be, if that shape remains in the mind, if the people, that dissuader from the honourable, does not at once intercept the notable impulse; few have been able to carry home the resolve they had conceived.

8. It is easy to rouse a hearer to a longing for what is right; for Nature has given to all the foundations and the seed of the virtues. We are all born for all these things; when an instigator approaches, then that good spirit, as if set free, is awakened. Do you not see how the theatres ring whenever something is said which we publicly acknowledge and by consent attest to be true?

9. "To poverty many things are lacking, to avarice all things." "The miser is good to no one, but worst of all to himself." At these verses even the most sordid man applauds and rejoices that reproach is cast upon his own faults; how much more, do you judge, does this come about when such things are said by a philosopher, when verses are inserted among wholesome precepts, to sink those same lessons more effectively into the minds of the untaught?

10. For, as Cleanthes used to say, just as our breath gives back a clearer sound when the trumpet, drawing it through the narrows of a long pipe, has at last poured it out at a wider opening, so the tight necessity of verse makes our meanings clearer. The same things are heard more carelessly and strike less, so long as they are said in loose prose; but when measures have been added and fixed feet have bound up an excellent meaning, that same sentiment is hurled, as it were, from a more vigorous arm.

11. Much is said about the contempt of money, and it is taught in the longest discourses that men should think their riches to lie in the mind, not in their estate, that he is wealthy who is fitted to his own poverty and has made himself rich with little; yet our minds are struck more when verses of this sort are spoken: "That mortal needs least who desires least." "He has what he wishes, who can wish for what is enough."

12. When we hear these and the like, we are led to a confession of the truth. For those to whom nothing is enough marvel, cry aloud, and proclaim hatred of money. When you have seen this feeling in them, press on, urge this, lay this load on, leaving aside ambiguities and syllogisms and quibbles and the rest of the toys of useless cleverness. Speak against avarice, speak against luxury; when you have seen that you have made progress and have stirred the minds of the hearers, press in more vehemently; it is past belief how much such a discourse profits when it is aimed at a cure and wholly turned to the good of the hearers. For tender natures are most easily won over to the love of the honourable and the right, and truth lays its hand upon those still teachable and lightly corrupted, if it has found a fitting advocate.

13. I at least, when I used to hear Attalus declaiming against vices, against errors, against the evils of life, often pitied the human race, and believed him to be sublime and higher than the summit of mankind. He himself said that he was a king, but he seemed to me to be more than a king, since he was permitted to exercise censorship over those who reign.

14. But when he had begun to commend poverty and to show that whatever exceeds use is a superfluous burden, heavy to the bearer, I often longed to go forth from the school a poor man. When he had begun to expose our pleasures, to praise a chaste body, a sober table, a mind pure not only from forbidden pleasures but even from superfluous ones, it pleased me to set bounds to my throat and belly.

15. Hence certain things have remained with me, Lucilius. For I had come to all of them with a great onset. Then, brought back to the life of the city, I kept few of what I had begun well. Hence oysters and mushrooms were renounced for my whole life; for they are not foods, but allurements, forcing the already sated to eat, which is most welcome to gluttons and to those who stuff themselves beyond what they can hold; easy to go down, easy to come back up.

16. Hence for my whole life I abstain from perfume, since the best scent on the body is none. Hence the stomach free of wine. Hence for my whole life I flee the bath; to boil the body down and exhaust it with sweats I believed both useless and effeminate. The rest of the things I had cast off have returned, yet in such a way that, of things whose abstinence I broke off, I keep a measure—and one indeed very near to abstinence, perhaps even more difficult, since some things are cut off more easily by the mind than tempered.

17. Since I have begun to set forth to you with how much greater an onset I came to philosophy as a youth than I go on with it as an old man, I shall not be ashamed to confess what love Pythagoras instilled in me. Sotion used to tell why Pythagoras abstained from animals, and why later Sextius did. The reason was different for each, but for each magnificent.

18. Sextius believed that man had enough of nourishment short of blood, and that a habit of cruelty arose where the tearing of flesh had been brought into a pleasure. He added that the materials of luxury must be cut down; he concluded that varied foods, foreign to our bodies, were contrary to good health.

19. But Pythagoras said that there was a kinship of all things with all, and a commerce of souls passing into one shape and another. No soul, if you believe him, perishes, nor even ceases save for a brief time, while it is poured over into another body. We shall see through what turns of time and when, after wandering through several dwellings, it returns into a man; in the meantime he made men fear crime and parricide, since they might, unaware, run upon the soul of a parent and violate it with the knife or the tooth, if in some creature there lodged a kindred spirit.

20. When Sotion had set forth these things and filled them out with his arguments, "Do you not believe," he said, "that souls are assigned to one body after another, and that what we call death is a migration? Do you not believe that in these herds or wild beasts, or in creatures plunged in water, there lingers the soul that was once a man's? Do you not believe that nothing perishes in this world, but only changes its region? And that not only the heavenly bodies are turned through fixed circuits, but that living things too pass in turn, and souls are driven round the cycle? Great men have believed these things."

21. And so suspend your judgement, but keep everything for yourself an open question. If these things are true, to have abstained from animals is innocence; if false, it is frugality. What loss to your credulity is there in this? I am snatching from you the food of lions and vultures.

22. Stirred by these things, I began to abstain from animals, and at the end of a year the habit was not only easy for me, but sweet. I believed my mind to be more active, and I would not affirm to you today whether it was. You ask how I left off? The time of my youth had fallen in the early principate of Tiberius Caesar. Foreign rites were then being expelled, but among the proofs of superstition was set down abstinence from certain animals. And so, at my father's request—who did not fear slander, but hated philosophy—I returned to my former habit. Nor did he persuade me with difficulty to begin dining better.

23. Attalus used to praise a mattress that resisted the body; such I use even as an old man, one in which no imprint can appear. I have related these things to prove to you how vehement an impulse young recruits have toward all that is best, if someone exhorts them, if someone sets them on fire. But some fault is committed through the fault of the teachers, who teach us to dispute, not to live; and some through the fault of the learners, who bring to their teachers a purpose not of cultivating the mind, but the wit. And so what was philosophy has been made philology.

24. But it matters much with what purpose you approach any subject. He who is going to be a grammarian and examines Virgil reads that excellent line, "irrecoverable time flees on," not with this mind: we must watch; unless we make haste, we shall be left behind; the swift day drives us and is driven; we are snatched along unawares; we arrange everything for the future and amid headlong things are slow; but he reads it to observe how often Virgil, when he speaks of the swiftness of the seasons, uses this word "flees." "The best days for wretched mortals flee first; on come diseases and gloomy old age and toil, and the cruelty of harsh death snatches them away."

25. But he who looks to philosophy brings these same lines to the use he ought: "Virgil," he says, "never says the days go, but flee, which is the most rapid kind of running, and that all the best things are first snatched away; why then do we delay to rouse ourselves, that we may be able to match the speed of a most rapid thing? The better things fly past, the worse come on."

26. Just as from a jar what is first to flow out is the purest, and all that is heaviest and most turbid settles to the bottom, so in our span of life what is best is in the first part. Do we allow that to be drained off by others, while we keep the dregs for ourselves? Let this cling to the mind and please us as though sent from an oracle: "The best days for wretched mortals flee first."

27. Why best? Because what remains is uncertain. Why best? Because as young men we can learn, can turn a mind still pliant and tractable to better things; because this time is fit for labours, fit for plying our wits with studies and exercising our bodies with works; what remains is more sluggish and more languid and nearer the end. Therefore let us do this with our whole mind, and, laying aside the things to which we turn off, let us labour at the one thing, lest, being left behind, we at last understand this speed of most fleeting time, which we cannot hold back. Let each first day, as if it were the best, please us and be reduced into our possession.

28. What flees must be seized. The man who reads that verse with the eyes of a grammarian does not reflect on this—that each best day is first because diseases come on, because old age presses, and hangs over the head even of those still thinking of adolescence; but he says that Virgil always sets diseases and old age together, and not, by Hercules, without reason. For old age is an incurable disease.

29. "Besides," he says, "Virgil has given old age this surname, he calls it 'gloomy': 'on come diseases and gloomy old age.' In another place he says: 'pale Diseases dwell, and gloomy Old Age.'" There is no reason for you to wonder that each gathers from the same material things suited to his own pursuits; in the same meadow the ox seeks grass, the dog the hare, the stork the lizard.

30. When some philologist takes up Cicero's book On the Commonwealth, here, and a grammarian there, and there one devoted to philosophy, each directs his attention elsewhere. The philosopher marvels that so much could be said against justice. When the philologist comes to this same reading, he notes this down: that there were two Roman kings, of whom the one had no father, the other no mother. For there is doubt about the mother of Servius; Ancus is said to have had no father, being the grandson of Numa.

31. Besides he notes that the man whom we call dictator, and whom we read so named in the histories, was among the ancients called master of the people. To this day it stands so in the books of the augurs, and the proof is that the man named by him is master of the horse. Equally he notes that Romulus perished during an eclipse of the sun; that there was an appeal to the people even from the kings; that this is so in the books of the pontiffs, and others think so, and Fenestella too.

32. When a grammarian unfolds the same books, first he puts down in his commentary that the word reapse is used by Cicero, that is, re ipsa, "in fact itself," and no less sepse, that is, se ipse, "himself." Then he passes to those things which the custom of the age has changed, as when Cicero says: "since by his interruption we have been called back from the very calx." This, which we now call in the circus creta (the chalk-line), the ancients called calx (the lime-line).

33. Then he gathers the verses of Ennius, and first of all those written about Africanus: "to whom no citizen nor enemy will be able to render a reward worthy of his deeds." From this he says he understands that ops among the ancients did not mean only "aid," but "service." For Ennius says that no one, neither citizen nor enemy, could render Scipio a reward worthy of his service.

34. Then he thinks himself fortunate that he has found whence it seemed good to Virgil to say: "over whom the huge gate of heaven thunders." Ennius, he says, filched this from Homer, and Virgil from Ennius. For there is in Cicero, in these very books On the Commonwealth, this epigram of Ennius: "If it is right for anyone to ascend to the regions of the heavenly ones, for me alone the great gate of heaven lies open."

35. But, that I myself, while I do something else, may not slip into being a philologist or a grammarian, I give this warning: that the hearing and reading of philosophers should be turned to the purpose of the happy life, not that we may hunt for ancient or coined words, or improper metaphors and figures of speech, but for precepts that will profit and for magnificent and spirited utterances, which may soon be transferred into action. Let us so learn these things that what have been words may become works.

36. But I judge that no men deserve worse of all mortals than those who have learned philosophy as though it were some saleable craft, who live otherwise than they teach men ought to live. For they carry themselves about as examples of a useless discipline, liable to every vice which they pursue with words.

37. No such teacher can profit me any more than a helmsman who is seasick in a storm. The helm must be held while the wave snatches it, one must struggle with the very sea, the sails must be wrenched from the wind; what help to me can be a steersman of the ship who is dumbstruck and vomiting? How much greater a storm do you think life is tossed by than any vessel? One must not talk, but steer.

38. Everything they say, everything they fling about with the crowd listening, is borrowed: Plato said those things, Zeno said them, Chrysippus and Posidonius and a vast army of our school, so many and such men. How they can prove these things to be their own, I will show: let them do what they have said.

39. Since I have now said what I wished to convey to you, I will now satisfy your desire, and will transfer entire into another letter the matter you had demanded, lest you come weary to a thorny subject, one to be heard with ears erect and curious. Farewell.

1. You wish me to write to you what I think of this question that is bandied about among our school: whether justice, courage, prudence, and the other virtues are living creatures. By this subtlety, dearest Lucilius, we have brought it about that we seem to exercise our wits among trifles and to waste our leisure on disputations that will profit nothing. I will do what you wish, and will set forth what our school thinks. But I declare that I am of another opinion: I think there are certain things that befit a man in Greek slippers and Greek cloak. So let me tell you what it is that moved the ancients, or what the ancients have moved.

2. It is agreed that the mind is a living creature, since it is the very thing that makes us living creatures, since from it living creatures have drawn this name. But virtue is nothing else than the mind in a certain condition; therefore it is a living creature. Next, virtue does something; but nothing can be done without impulse. If it has impulse, which belongs to nothing save a living creature, it is a living creature. "If virtue is a living creature," he says, "it has virtue itself."

3. Why should it not have itself? Just as the wise man does all things through virtue, so virtue acts through itself. "Therefore," he says, "all the arts too are living creatures, and all the things we think and grasp with the mind." It follows that many thousands of living creatures dwell in these narrow quarters of the breast, and that we are each many living creatures or have many living creatures. You ask what is answered against this? Each one of those things will be a living creature; they will not be many living creatures. Why? I will tell you, if you lend me your subtlety and your attention.

4. Single living creatures must have single substances; all those things have one mind; and so they can be single, they cannot be many. I am both an animal and a man, yet you will not say that we are two. Why? Because they ought to be separate. So I say: the one ought to be sundered from the other, that they may be two. Whatever is manifold in one falls under one nature; and so it is one.

5. Both my mind is a living creature and I am a living creature, yet we are not two. Why? Because my mind is a part of me. A thing will be counted by itself only when it stands by itself. But where it will be a member of another, it cannot be seen as a separate thing. Why? I will tell you: because that which is a separate thing must be its own and proper and whole and complete within itself.

6. I have declared that I am of another opinion. For not only will the virtues be living creatures, if this be accepted, but also the vices opposed to them and the passions, such as anger, fear, grief, suspicion. This thing will go further: all opinions, all thoughts will be living creatures. Which must in no way be accepted. For not whatever is done by a man is a man.

7. "What is justice?" he says. "The mind in a certain condition. And so, if the mind is a living creature, so is justice." By no means. For this is a habit of the mind and a certain force; the same mind is turned into various shapes and is not so many times a different living creature as it does a different thing. Nor is that which is done by the mind a living creature.

8. If justice is a living creature, if courage is, if the other virtues are, do they cease to be living creatures and then again presently begin, or are they always so? The virtues cannot cease. Therefore many living creatures, nay innumerable ones, dwell in this one mind.

9. "They are not many," he says, "because they are bound together out of one and are the parts and members of one." We picture to ourselves, then, such a face of the mind as the hydra has, which has many heads, each of which fights by itself and harms by itself. And yet none of those heads is a living creature, but the head of a living creature, while the hydra itself is one living creature. No one has said that in the Chimaera the lion is a living creature or the dragon; these were its parts; but parts are not living creatures. What is it from which you conclude that justice is a living creature?

10. "It does something," he says, "and is of profit. But what does something and is of profit has impulse; and what has impulse is a living creature." It is true, if it has its own impulse; but it has not its own, but the mind's.

11. Every living creature, until it dies, is what it began as; a man, until he dies, is a man, a horse a horse, a dog a dog. It cannot pass into something else. Justice, that is, the mind in a certain condition, is a living creature. Let us grant it; then courage is a living creature, that is, the mind in a certain condition. What mind? The one that just now was justice? It is held fast in the former living creature, it is not permitted to pass into another living creature; it must persist in that in which it first began to be.

12. Besides, one mind cannot belong to two living creatures, much less to several. If justice, courage, temperance, and the other virtues are living creatures, how will they have one mind? They must have single ones, or they are not living creatures.

13. One body cannot belong to several living creatures. This even they themselves admit. What is the body of justice? The mind. What? What is the body of courage? The same mind. And yet one body cannot belong to two living creatures.

14. "But the same mind," he says, "puts on the habit of justice and of courage and of temperance." This could happen, if at the time when there was justice there was no courage, at the time when there was courage there was no temperance; but as it is, all the virtues are present at once. So how will they singly be living creatures, since there is one mind, which cannot make more than one living creature?

15. Finally, no living creature is a part of another living creature. But justice is a part of the mind; therefore it is not a living creature. I seem to myself to be wasting my labour on a thing already admitted; for one ought rather to be indignant about this than to dispute it. No living creature is equal to another. Look round at the bodies of all things: not one but has its own colour and its own shape and its own size.

16. Among the other things on account of which the genius of the divine craftsman is marvellous, I count this too, that in so great an abundance of things he has never lighted upon the same thing twice; even the things that seem alike, when you have compared them, are different. He has made so many kinds of leaves: not one but is stamped with its own property. So many living creatures: the size of none agrees with another, there is always some difference. He demanded of himself that the things which were separate should also be unlike and unequal; but all the virtues, as you say, are equal. Therefore they are not living creatures.

17. Every living creature acts of itself. But virtue does nothing of itself, but together with a man. All living creatures are either rational, like men and gods, or irrational, like wild beasts and cattle. The virtues are certainly rational; and yet they are neither men nor gods; therefore they are not living creatures.

18. Every rational living creature does nothing unless it has first been stirred by the appearance of some thing, then has taken up an impulse, then assent has confirmed this impulse. I will tell you what assent is. I ought to walk: then at last I walk, when I have said this to myself and approved this opinion of mine. I ought to sit: then at last I sit. This assent is not in virtue.

19. For suppose virtue to be prudence; how will it assent: I ought to walk? Nature does not admit this. For prudence looks out for him whose it is, not for itself. For it can neither walk nor sit. Therefore it has not assent; it is not a rational living creature. If virtue is a living creature, it is rational.

20. But it is not rational; therefore neither is it a living creature. If virtue is a living creature, and virtue is a good, is not every good a living creature? It is. Our school admit this. To save one's father is a good, and to deliver an opinion prudently in the senate is a good, and to give a just verdict is a good; therefore to save one's father is a living creature and to deliver an opinion prudently is a living creature. The matter has gone so far that you cannot hold your laughter: to keep silent prudently is a good, to dine frugally is a good; so both to keep silent and to dine are living creatures.

21. I, by Hercules, will not cease to tickle myself and to make sport of these subtle absurdities. Justice and courage, if they are living creatures, are certainly terrestrial. Every terrestrial living creature is cold, hungry, thirsty; therefore justice is cold, courage is hungry, mercy is thirsty.

22. What further? Shall I not ask them what shape those living creatures have? That of a man, or of a horse, or of a wild beast? If they give them a round shape, like that which they have given to God, I will ask whether avarice and luxury and madness are equally round. For these too are living creatures. If they round these off as well, I will still ask whether a prudent walk is a living creature. They must necessarily admit it, and then say that walking is a living creature, and a round one at that.

23. But that you may not think that I am the first of our school not to speak by prescription but to hold my own opinion: between Cleanthes and his pupil Chrysippus there is no agreement as to what walking is. Cleanthes says it is breath sent from the governing part down to the feet, Chrysippus says it is the governing part itself. Why then should not each man, by Chrysippus's own example, claim himself for himself, and laugh at those living creatures, so many that the world itself cannot contain them?

24. "The virtues," he says, "are not many living creatures, and yet they are living creatures. For just as someone is both a poet and an orator, and yet one man, so those virtues are living creatures, but are not many. The mind is the same, and is both a mind and just and prudent and brave, being in a certain condition with regard to each single virtue."

25. The controversy is removed; we are agreed. For I too meanwhile admit that the mind is a living creature, intending to pass my verdict on that matter later; but I deny that its actions are living creatures. Otherwise all words too will be living creatures and all verses; for if prudent speech is a good, and every good is a living creature, then speech is a living creature. A prudent verse is a good, and every good is a living creature; therefore a verse is a living creature. So "Arms and the man I sing" is a living creature, which they cannot call round, since it has six feet.

26. "A spider's web, by Hercules, is the whole of this thing now being discussed." I burst with laughter when I picture to myself that a solecism is a living creature, and a barbarism, and a syllogism, and that, like a painter, I assign fitting faces to them. Are these the things we discuss with knitted brows, with wrinkled forehead? I cannot in this place help quoting Caelius's words: "O dismal trifles!" They are ridiculous. Why, then, do we not rather treat of something useful to us and wholesome, and inquire how we may be able to reach the virtues, what road may lead us to them?

27. Teach me, not whether courage is a living creature, but that no living creature is happy without courage, unless it has grown strong against the strokes of chance and has, by pondering them, mastered beforehand every accident before it should befall. What is courage? The impregnable bulwark of human weakness; he who has set it round himself holds out untroubled in this siege of life; for he uses his own strength, his own weapons.

28. At this point I wish to report to you the sentiment of our Posidonius: "There is no reason for you to think yourself ever safe in the arms of fortune; fight with your own. Fortune does not arm us against herself; and so men furnished against their enemies are unarmed against her."

29. Alexander indeed ravaged and put to flight the Persians and Hyrcanians and Indians and whatever nations the East extends as far as the ocean, but he himself, now having slain a friend, now having lost one, lay in the darkness, mourning at one time his crime, at another his loss, the conqueror of so many kings and peoples succumbing to anger and grief. For he had laboured to have all things rather than his passions in his power.

30. Oh, by how great errors are men possessed, who long to extend their right of dominion across the seas, and judge themselves most fortunate if they hold many provinces with their soldiery and add new ones to the old, ignorant of what that mighty realm, equal to the gods, may be!

31. To rule oneself is the greatest dominion. Let philosophy teach me how sacred a thing is justice, which looks to another's good and seeks nothing for itself save the use of itself. Let it have nothing to do with ambition and fame; let it please itself. Let each man before all things persuade himself of this: I ought to be just for nothing. It is too little; let him further persuade himself of this: let it delight me to spend myself freely upon this most beautiful virtue. Let his whole thought be turned as far as possible from private advantages. There is no reason for you to look to what the reward of a just deed may be; there is a greater one in the just deed itself. Fix this still upon yourself, what I was saying a little before: it does not matter to the case how many know your fairness.

32. He who wishes his own virtue to be made public labours not for virtue but for glory. Will you not be just without glory? But, by Hercules, you will often have to be just with infamy. And then, if you are wise, let an ill repute well earned delight you. Farewell.

1. I would not have you too anxious about words and composition, my dear Lucilius; I have greater things for you to care about. Ask what you are to write, not how; and even this, not that you may write it, but that you may feel it, that those things you have felt you may the more apply to yourself and, as it were, set your seal upon them. Whosoever's speech you see to be over-careful and polished, know that his mind too is no less taken up with petty things.

2. A great man speaks more carelessly and with more security; whatever he says has more of confidence than of pains. You know the trim young men, sleek of beard and hair, fresh from the band-box; you would hope nothing from them strong, nothing solid. Speech is the dress of the mind: if it is clipped round and rouged and made up by hand, it shows that the mind too is not sincere and has something cracked in it. Neatness is no manly ornament.

3. If it were permitted us to look into the mind of a good man, oh, what a fair face we should see, how holy, how shining with a magnificent calm—here justice gleaming, there courage, here temperance and prudence! And besides these, frugality and self-control and endurance and liberality and courtesy and—who would believe it?—a good rare in man, humanity, would shed their splendour upon it. Then would foresight together with refinement, and, springing from these, magnanimity most eminent, how much beauty, good gods, how much weight and dignity would they add to it! How great, with what charm, would be its authority! No one would call it lovable who would not at the same time call it venerable.

4. If anyone saw this face, loftier and more shining than is wont to be seen among human things, would he not halt, stupefied as though at the meeting of a divinity, and silently pray that it might be lawful to have seen it? Then, drawn on by the very kindness of its countenance calling him forth, would he not worship and entreat, and, long contemplating it, much towering and uplifted beyond the measure of what we are wont to look upon among us, with eyes blazing with a gentle yet none the less living fire—then at last would he not utter, in awe and astonishment, that saying of our Virgil?

5. "Oh, how shall I name you, maiden? For your face is not mortal, nor does your voice sound human. Be propitious, and lighten our toil, whoever you are." She will be present and will lighten it, if we are willing to worship her. But she is worshipped not by the slaughter of fat bulls' bodies, nor by gold and silver hung up, nor by coin poured into her treasury, but by a pious and upright will.

6. No one, I say, would not burn with love of her, if it fell to us to see her; for now many things hinder, and either dazzle our gaze with too great a splendour or hold it back in obscurity. But if, just as the sight of the eyes is wont to be sharpened and cleared by certain medicines, so we are willing to free the keen sight of the mind from its impediments, we shall be able to discern virtue even when it is buried in the body, even when poverty stands in the way, even when lowliness and infamy lie before it. We shall behold, I say, that beauty, however covered by what is sordid.

7. Conversely, we shall likewise perceive wickedness and the lethargy of a wretched mind, however much the splendour about it of radiant riches may hinder, and the false light, on this side of honours, on that of great powers, may beat upon the beholder.

8. Then it will be permitted us to understand how worthless are the things we admire, most like children, to whom every plaything is of value; for they prefer to their parents, and no less to their brothers, necklaces bought for a small coin. What then, as Ariston says, is the difference between us and them, save that we go mad over pictures and statues, fools at a dearer rate? Pebbles found on the shore, smooth and having some variety, delight them; us the spots of huge columns, whether brought from the sands of Egypt or from the deserts of Africa to support some portico or some dining-hall capacious enough for a populace.

9. We admire walls overlaid with thin marble, though we know what it is that is concealed beneath. We impose upon our own eyes, and when we have flooded our ceilings with gold, what else do we rejoice in but a lie? For we know that under that gold ugly timbers lie hidden. Nor is it only upon walls or ceilings that a thin ornament is stretched in front; the happiness of all those men whom you see walking on high is gilt foil. Look closely, and you will know how much evil lies beneath that thin film of dignity.

10. This very thing which holds so many magistrates, so many judges, which both makes magistrates and makes judges—money—ever since it began to be in honour, the true honour of things has fallen, and, made by turns merchants and merchandise, we ask not of what sort each thing is, but at what price; we are dutiful for a fee, undutiful for a fee, and we follow honourable things only so long as some hope is in them, ready to pass over to the contrary if crimes shall promise more.

11. Our parents have instilled in us an admiration of gold and silver, and the craving poured in while we were tender has settled deeper and grown up with us. Then the whole people, discordant in other things, agrees in this; this they look up to, this they wish for their own, this they dedicate to the gods, as though it were the greatest of human things, when they wish to seem grateful. In short, morals have been brought to such a pass that poverty is a thing of curse and reproach, despised by the rich, hateful to the poor.

12. Then come in besides the verses of the poets, which apply a torch to our passions, in which riches are praised as though they were the one glory and ornament of life. To them the immortal gods seem able to give and to have nothing better.

13. "The palace of the Sun was high with lofty columns, bright with flashing gold." Look at his chariot too: "The axle was of gold, the pole of gold, of gold the rim of the topmost wheel, and the row of spokes of silver." In short, the age that men wish to seem the best they call golden.

14. Nor among the Greek tragedians are there lacking those who barter innocence, safety, a good name, for gain. "Let me be called most base, so I be called rich." "Whether he be rich, we all ask; whether good, no one. Not for what reason or whence, only what you have, do they ask. Everywhere each man has been worth as much as he had. What is it shameful for us to have? Nothing. Either I choose to live rich or to die poor. He dies well, whoever dies while making gain." "Money, the mighty good of the human race, to which neither a mother's pleasure can be equal, nor a fawning child's, nor a father holy by his deserts; if anything so sweet shines in the face of Venus, deservedly does money move the loves of gods and men."

15. When these last verses had been pronounced in a tragedy of Euripides, the whole people rose up with one impulse to cast out both the actor and the play, until Euripides himself sprang forth into the midst, asking them to wait and to see what end this admirer of gold would make. In that play Bellerophon was paying the penalty which each man pays in his own.

16. For no avarice is without penalty, although avarice is itself penalty enough. Oh, how many tears, how many toils it demands! How wretched is it in its cravings, how wretched in its gains! Add the daily anxieties which torture each man in proportion to his holdings. Money is possessed with greater torment than it is sought. How men groan over their losses, which both fall heavy and seem heavier! In short, though fortune take nothing from them, whatever is not acquired is a loss.

17. "But men call that man happy and rich, and pray to attain as much as he possesses." I admit it. What then? Do you think any men of a worse condition than those who have both misery and envy? Would that those who are going to wish for riches would take counsel with the rich! Would that those going to seek honours would take counsel with the ambitious and with those who have attained the highest grade of dignity! Assuredly they would have changed their prayers, while these meanwhile take up new ones, though they have condemned their former. For there is no one whom his own good fortune, even if it came at a run, satisfies. Men complain both of their plans and of their advancements, and always prefer what they have left behind.

18. Therefore this is what philosophy will furnish you, than which I count nothing greater: you will never repent of yourself. To this so solid a happiness, which no storm may shake, words aptly woven together and speech flowing gently will not lead you. Let them go as they will, provided the mind keeps its own composure, provided it be great and unconcerned about opinions, and pleasing to itself because of the very things that displease others; one that estimates its own progress by its life, and judges that it knows just so much as it neither desires nor fears. Farewell.

1. The day has now felt its loss. It has rebounded somewhat, yet so that there is still a liberal space, if a man rises with the day itself, so to speak. He is more dutiful and better who awaits the day and catches the first light; base is he who lies half-asleep when the sun is high, whose waking begins at midday; and to many even this is before dawn.

2. There are those who have reversed the offices of day and night, and do not open their eyes, heavy with yesterday's debauch, before night begins to come on. Such as the condition is said to be of those whom Nature, as Virgil says, has placed beneath our seats on the opposite side—"and when the first Dawn breathes upon us with her panting horses, for them the reddening Evening-star kindles his late lamps"—such is the life, not the region, of these men, contrary to all. There are certain antipodes in the very same city, who, as Marcus Cato says, have never seen either the rising or the setting sun.

3. Do you think that these men know how one should live, who do not know when? And do these men fear death, in which they have buried themselves while still alive? They are as ill-omened as night-birds. Though they pass their darkness in wine and perfume, though they draw out the whole time of their perverse waking in feasts, and those cooked down into many courses, they do not banquet, but make their own funeral rites. The dead, at least, have their offerings paid by day. But, by Hercules, no day is long to a man who is doing something. Let us extend life; its duty and its proof is action. Let the night be cut short, and let something of it be transferred to the day.

4. Fowls that are got ready for banquets, that, kept motionless, they may fatten easily, are kept in the dark; so, to those who lie without any exercise, a swelling invades the sluggish body, and an idle plumpness grows upon them in their proud shade. But the bodies of these men, who have dedicated themselves to darkness, are foul to look upon. Indeed, their colour is more suspect than that of those suffering from a disease; pale they are, languid and faded, and in the living the flesh is that of a corpse. Yet I should call this the least of the evils in them. How much more darkness is there in the mind! That is stunned within itself, that is darkened, it envies the blind. Who ever had eyes for the sake of darkness?

5. You ask how this perversity comes upon the mind, of turning away from the day and transferring the whole of life into the night? All vices fight against Nature, all forsake the due order. This is the aim of luxury, to rejoice in things perverse, and not only to depart from the right, but to go as far as possible away, and then even to stand in its very contrary.

6. Do they not seem to you to live against Nature who drink fasting, who take wine into empty veins and pass over to food drunk? And yet this is a frequent vice of young men, who cultivate their strength, so that almost on the very threshold of the bath they drink among the naked, nay, carouse, and then again and again scrape off the sweat which they have raised by their frequent and heated draughts. To drink after luncheon or dinner is vulgar; this rustic heads of families do, and men ignorant of true pleasure. That unmixed wine delights them which does not float upon food, which penetrates freely to the sinews; that intoxication pleases which comes into an empty place.

7. Do they not seem to you to live against Nature who exchange their dress with women? Do they not live against Nature who strive that boyhood may shine at an age not its own? What can be done more cruel or more wretched? Will he never be a man, that he may long endure a man? And when his sex ought to have rescued him from outrage, will not even his age rescue him?

8. Do they not live against Nature who long for the rose in winter, and by a fomentation of warm waters and an apt change of heat force forth in midwinter the lily, a flower of spring? Do they not live against Nature who plant orchards on the tops of towers? Whose woods wave on the roofs and gables of houses, their roots springing from a place to which they would have wickedly thrust their tops? Do they not live against Nature who lay the foundations of baths in the sea, and do not think they swim daintily enough unless their heated pools are beaten by wave and tempest?

9. When they have made it their rule to wish all things contrary to the custom of Nature, at last they grow wholly unaccustomed to her. It is light: it is the time for sleep. It is quiet: now let us be exercised, now let us be driven about, now let us lunch. Now the daylight draws nearer: it is the time for dinner. One must not do what the people does. It is a sordid thing to live by the worn and common road. Let the public day be abandoned: let a morning of our own and peculiar to us be made for us.

10. These men are to me in the place of the dead. For how little are they removed from a funeral, and a bitter one at that, who live by torches and tapers? We remember that many lived this life at the same time, among them Acilius Buta, a man of praetorian rank, to whom, after a huge patrimony had been consumed, when he confessed his poverty, Tiberius said: "You have awakened too late."

11. Julius Montanus was reciting a poem, a tolerable poet and known both for the friendship of Tiberius and for his coldness. Risings and settings of the sun he most gladly inserted. And so, when a certain man was indignant that he had recited the whole day and declared that one should not go to his recitations, Pinarius Natta said: "I can never act more liberally: I am ready to hear him from rising to setting."

12. When he had recited these verses—"Phoebus begins to bring forth his burning flames, the ruddy day to spread itself; now the sad swallow, returning, begins to bring food to her shrill nestlings, and shares it out, serving it from her soft beak"—Varus, a Roman knight, a companion of Marcus Vinicius, an attender of good dinners, which he earned by the wickedness of his tongue, exclaimed: "Buta is beginning to sleep." Then, when he had presently recited:

13. "Now the shepherds have placed their herds in the stalls, now sluggish night begins to give silence to the drowsing lands," the same Varus said: "What do you say? Is it night already? I will go and pay my respects to Buta." Nothing was more notorious than this life of his, turned about into the contrary; which, as I said, many lived at the same time.

14. But the reason for living so is, for some, not that they think the night itself has anything more pleasant, but that nothing accustomed pleases them, and the light is grievous to a bad conscience, and to one craving or despising all things, according as they have been bought at a great price or a small, the daylight, which costs nothing, is wearisome. Besides, the luxurious wish that their life should be talked of while they live; for if there is silence, they think they are wasting their labour. And so they are ill at ease whenever they do anything that may escape report. Many devour their estates, many keep mistresses. To get a name among these men, you must do a thing not only luxurious, but notable; in a city so busy, ordinary wickedness finds no gossip.

15. We had heard Pedo Albinovanus relating—and he was a most elegant teller of tales—that he had lived above the house of Sextus Papinius. He was one of this crowd of light-shunners. "I hear," he said, "about the third hour of the night the sound of whips. I ask what he is doing; he is said to be going over his accounts. I hear about the sixth hour of the night an excited shouting; I ask what it is; he is said to be exercising his voice. I ask about the eighth hour of the night what that noise of wheels means; he is said to be taking a drive."

16. "About daybreak there is a running to and fro, the slaves are called, the butlers, the cooks are in an uproar. I ask what it is; he is said to have called for mead and barley-water, to have come out of the bath." "His dinner," he said, "by no means exceeded the day, for he lived very frugally; he consumed nothing but the night." And so, when certain men said that he was greedy and sordid, "You," he said, "will call him a lamp-liver too."

17. You should not wonder if you find such great peculiarities of the vices; they are various, they have innumerable faces, their kinds cannot be comprehended. Simple is the care of the right, manifold that of the wrong, and it admits of ever so many new deviations. The same befalls morals; those of men who follow Nature are easy, are free, have slight differences; the morals of these distorted men are most at variance both with all others and among themselves.

18. Yet the chief cause of this disease seems to me to be a disdain of the common life. As they distinguish themselves from the rest by their dress, by the elegance of their dinners, by the neatness of their carriages, so they wish to separate themselves also by the arrangement of their hours. They are unwilling to sin in the usual way, who have for the reward of their sinning infamy. This all these men seek who, so to speak, live backwards.

19. Therefore, Lucilius, we must keep to the road that Nature has prescribed, and not turn aside from it; for those who follow it all things are easy and ready, but for those who strive against it there is no other life than that of men rowing against the stream. Farewell.

1. You desire to know what I think about the liberal studies. I admire none of them, I count none among the goods, which has money for its end. They are hireling trades, useful so far as they prepare the mind, not detain it. For we must dwell on these things only so long as the mind can do nothing greater; they are our apprenticeship, not our work.

2. Why the liberal studies are so called you see; because they are worthy of a free man. But there is in truth one study that is liberal, the one that makes a man free. This is the study of wisdom, lofty, brave, great-souled. The rest are petty and childish; or do you believe there is any good in those things whose professors you behold to be the basest of all men and the most disgraceful? We ought not to be learning those things, but to have learned them. Some have judged that this should be asked about the liberal studies, whether they make a man good; but they do not even promise it, nor lay claim to the knowledge of this matter.

3. The grammarian is occupied with the care of language, and, if he wishes to range more widely, with histories, and, to push his bounds out as far as possible, with poems. Which of these paves a way to virtue? The parsing of syllables, and care over words, and the memorizing of fables, and the law and metre of verses? Which of these takes away fear, removes desire, bridles lust?

4. Let us pass to geometry and music; you will find nothing in them that forbids you to fear, forbids you to desire. And whoever does not know these will know other things to no purpose. Let us see whether these men teach virtue or not. If they teach it, they are philosophers. But if they do not teach it, why are they called liberal studies?

5. Unless perhaps they persuade you that Homer was a philosopher, when they deny it by the very arguments by which they prove it. For now they make him a Stoic, approving virtue alone and shunning pleasures and not departing from the honourable even at the price of immortality; now an Epicurean, praising the state of a city at rest and one passing its life amid feasts and songs; now a Peripatetic, bringing in three kinds of goods; now an Academic, saying that all things are uncertain. It is plain that none of these is in him, because all of them are. For these things are at odds among themselves. Let us grant them that Homer was a philosopher; surely he became wise before he knew any poems. Therefore let us learn the things that made Homer wise.

6. For me to ask which was the elder, Homer or Hesiod, no more belongs to the matter than to know, since Hecuba was younger than Helen, why she bore her age so badly. What? Do you think it belongs to the matter to inquire into the ages of Patroclus and Achilles?

7. Do you ask where Ulysses wandered, rather than bring it about that we should not always be wandering? There is no leisure to hear whether he was tossed between Italy and Sicily, or outside the world known to us, for so long a wandering could not have been in so narrow a space; the storms of the mind toss us daily, and wickedness drives us into all the ills of Ulysses. There is no lack of beauty to disturb our eyes, no lack of an enemy; here are savage monsters that delight in human blood, here the treacherous flatteries of the ears, here shipwrecks and so many varieties of evils. Teach me this, how I may love my country, how my wife, how my father, how I may sail toward these things so honourable even after shipwreck.

8. Why do you inquire whether Penelope was chaste, whether she deceived her own age? Whether she suspected him to be Ulysses, before she knew it? Teach me what chastity is, and how great a good is in it, whether it is placed in the body or in the mind.

9. I pass to the musician: you teach me how high and low notes accord with one another, how a concord is made of strings rendering an unlike sound; rather make my mind accord with itself, and my counsels not be discordant. You show me which are the mournful modes; show me rather how, amid adversities, I may not let out a mournful cry.

10. The geometer teaches me to measure my broad estates, rather than teach me how I may measure how much is enough for a man. He teaches me to reckon, and lends my fingers to avarice, rather than teach me that these computations have nothing to do with the matter, that a man is not happier whose estate wearies the accountants; nay, how superfluous are the things he possesses who will be most unhappy if he is forced to reckon by himself how much he has.

11. What does it profit me to know how to divide a little field into parts, if I do not know how to divide it with my brother? What does it profit to gather up exactly the feet of an acre and to grasp even what has escaped the measuring-rod, if it makes me gloomy when an overbearing neighbour scrapes away something from my land? He teaches how I may lose nothing of my boundaries; but I wish to learn how to lose the whole of them cheerfully.

12. 'I am driven,' he says, 'from my father's and grandfather's field.' What? Before your grandfather who held that field? Can you explain whose, I do not say man's, but people's it was? You entered there not as owner, but as tenant. Whose tenant are you? If it goes well with you, your heir's. The lawyers deny that anything public can be acquired by use; this which you hold, which you call your own, is public, and indeed belongs to the human race.

13. O excellent art! You know how to measure round things, you reduce to a square whatever shape you have received, you tell the distances of the stars, there is nothing that does not fall under your measure. If you are an artist, measure a man's mind. Say how great it is, say how petty it is. You know what a straight line is; what does it profit you, if you do not know what is straight in life?

14. I come now to him who boasts of his knowledge of the heavens: 'whither the cold star of Saturn betakes itself, into what circles wanders the Cyllenian fire of heaven.' What will it profit to know this? That I should be anxious when Saturn and Mars stand opposed, or when Mercury makes his evening setting in the sight of Saturn, rather than learn this, that wherever those bodies are, they are propitious and cannot be changed?

15. An unbroken order of fates and an inevitable course drives them. They return through their fixed turns and either move or mark the effects of all things. But whether they make whatever happens, what will the knowledge of an unchangeable thing profit? Or whether they signify it, what does it matter to foresee what you cannot escape? Whether you know these things or do not know them, they will come to pass.

16. 'But if you look back to the swift sun and the stars that follow in order, never will tomorrow's hour deceive you, nor will you be ensnared by the treacheries of a cloudless night.' It has been provided fully and abundantly that I should be safe from snares.

17. Does not tomorrow's hour deceive me? For that deceives which befalls a man unawares. I do not know what will be; I know what may be. From this I shall despair of nothing, I await the whole; if anything is remitted, I count it gain. The hour deceives me if it spares me, but not even thus does it deceive me. For just as I know that all things can happen, so I know also that they will not necessarily happen. I await prosperity, I am prepared for adversity.

18. In this you must bear with me, that I do not go by the prescribed path. For I am not brought to receive painters into the number of the liberal arts, any more than statuaries or marble-workers or the other servants of luxury. Likewise I expel from these liberal studies wrestlers and the whole science that consists of oil and mud; or else I shall receive perfumers too, and cooks, and the rest who apply their wits to the service of our pleasures.

19. For what, I pray you, that is liberal have those fasting vomiters, whose bodies are in fattening and their minds in leanness and lethargy? Or do we believe that to be a liberal study for our youth, whom our ancestors trained upright, to throw javelins, to hurl the stake, to ride a horse, to handle arms? They taught their children nothing that had to be learned lying down. But neither these nor those teach or nourish virtue. For what does it profit to govern a horse and to temper his course with the rein, yet to be dragged away by the most unbridled passions? What does it profit to conquer many in wrestling or in boxing, yet to be conquered by anger?

20. What then? Do the liberal studies confer nothing on us? For other things much, for virtue nothing. For even those arts, avowedly mean, which consist of the hand, contribute very much to the equipment of life, yet do not belong to virtue. Why then do we educate our sons in the liberal studies? Not because they can give virtue, but because they prepare the mind for receiving virtue. Just as that first instruction, as the ancients called it, in letters, through which the elements are handed to boys, does not teach the liberal arts, but soon makes room for grasping them, so the liberal arts do not lead the mind to virtue, but clear the way for it.

21. Posidonius says there are four kinds of arts: there are the common and mean, there are the entertaining, there are the children's, and there are the liberal. The common are those of the craftsmen, which consist of the hand and are taken up for equipping life, in which there is no pretence of comeliness, none of the honourable.

22. The entertaining are those which aim at the pleasure of the eyes and ears. To these you may add the engineers who devise platforms rising of themselves, and floors silently mounting aloft, and other unexpected transformations, either of things that cohered gaping apart, or of things that stood apart coming together of their own accord, or of things that projected gradually settling into themselves. By these the eyes of the ignorant are struck; all sudden things are wondered at, because they do not know the causes.

23. The children's, and having something in common with the liberal, are those arts which the Greeks call enkyklious, but our people liberal. But the only truly liberal, or rather, to speak more truly, free, are those whose concern is virtue.

24. 'Just as,' he says, 'there is one part of philosophy that is natural, one moral, one rational, so this crowd of liberal arts too claims for itself a place in philosophy. When it comes to natural questions, one rests on the testimony of geometry; therefore it is a part of that which it helps.'

25. Many things help us and are not therefore parts of us; nay, if they were parts, they would not help us. Food is a help to the body, but is not a part of it. Geometry renders us some service; it is necessary to philosophy as the carpenter is to geometry; but the carpenter is not a part of geometry, nor is geometry of philosophy.

26. Besides, each has its own bounds. For the wise man both inquires into and knows the causes of natural things, whose numbers and measures the geometer pursues and computes. By what reasoning the heavenly bodies subsist, what their force is or their nature, the wise man knows; their courses and recoils and certain phenomena by which they descend and are lifted up and at times offer the appearance of standing still, though it is not allowed to the heavenly bodies to stand still, these the mathematician gathers.

27. What cause produces images in a mirror the wise man will know; the geometer can tell you how far the body ought to be from the image, and what shape of mirror renders what images. That the sun is great the philosopher will prove; how great it is, the mathematician, who proceeds by a certain practice and exercise; but in order to proceed he must obtain certain first principles. But that is not an art in its own right whose foundation is begged.

28. Philosophy asks nothing from another, it raises its whole structure from itself alone; mathematics, so to speak, is a thing of the surface, it builds on another's ground. It receives first principles, by whose favour it may come to further things. If it went by itself to the truth, if it could grasp the nature of the whole world, I should say it would confer much on our minds, which grow by the handling of celestial things and draw something from on high.

29. The mind is perfected by one thing only, the unalterable knowledge of good and evil, which belongs to philosophy alone; for no other art inquires into good and evil. Let me run through the several virtues. Bravery is the despiser of things to be feared; the things that are terrible, that send beneath the yoke our liberty, it scorns, challenges, breaks. 'Do the liberal studies strengthen this? Loyalty is the most sacred good of the human breast, which is forced by no necessity to deceive, corrupted by no reward. "Burn," it says, "strike, kill; I will not betray, but the more pain shall seek out the secrets, the deeper will I bury them." Can the liberal studies make these minds? Temperance commands the pleasures, some it hates and drives away, others it dispenses and reduces to a sound measure, nor does it ever come to them for their own sake. It knows that the best measure of things desired is to take not as much as you wish, but as much as you ought.

30. Humanity forbids us to be proud toward our fellows, forbids us to be grasping. In words, in deeds, in feelings it shows itself courteous and kind to all; it counts no man's evil its own; its own good it loves chiefly for this, that it will be the good of another. Do the liberal studies teach these manners? No more than they teach simplicity, than modesty and moderation, no more than frugality and thrift, no more than mercy, which spares another's blood as its own and knows that a man must not be prodigally used by a man.

31. 'Since you say,' he says, 'that one does not come to virtue without the liberal studies, how do you deny that they contribute nothing to virtue?' Because one does not come to virtue without food either, yet food does not belong to virtue. Timber contributes nothing to a ship, although a ship is not made except of timber. There is no reason, I say, why you should think anything is made by the aid of that without which it cannot be made.

32. Indeed it may even be said that one can come to wisdom without the liberal studies; for although virtue must be learned, yet it is not learned through these. What reason is there why I should think a man who does not know letters will not be wise, since wisdom is not in letters? It hands over things, not words, and I know not whether the memory is not surer which has no support outside itself.

33. Wisdom is a great and spacious thing. It needs empty room. One must learn about things divine and human, about the past and the future, about things perishable and eternal, about time. Concerning this one thing alone, see how many questions are asked: first, whether it is anything in itself; then, whether anything is before time and without time; whether it began with the world, or, because there was something even before the world, time too existed.

34. There are countless questions about the soul alone: whence it is, what it is, when it begins to be, how long it is; whether it passes from one place to another and changes its dwelling, transferred into the shapes of other animals one after another, or serves only once and then, set free, wanders through the universe; whether it is body or not; what it will do when it ceases to act through us; how it will use its freedom when it has fled this prison; whether it forgets things past and then begins to know itself, when, parted from the body, it has withdrawn on high.

35. Whatever part of things human and divine you grasp, you will be wearied by a vast abundance of things to be inquired into and learned. That these things, so many, so great, may have a free lodging, the superfluous must be cleared from the mind. Virtue will not give itself into these straits; a great thing requires a roomy space. Let all things be expelled, let the whole breast be free for it.

36. 'But the knowledge of many arts delights one.' Therefore let us retain only as much of them as is necessary. Or do you think the man worthy of blame who gets together superfluous things for use and spreads out in his house a parade of costly objects, but do not think that man so who is busied with the superfluous furniture of letters? To wish to know more than is enough is a kind of intemperance.

37. And what of this, that this pursuit of the liberal arts makes men troublesome, wordy, ill-timed, pleased with themselves, and for this reason not learning the necessary things, that they have learned the superfluous? The grammarian Didymus wrote four thousand books. I should pity him, had he merely read so many superfluous ones. In these books it is inquired what was Homer's country, in these who was the true mother of Aeneas, in these whether Anacreon lived more lustfully or more drunkenly, in these whether Sappho was a public woman, and other things which, if you knew them, you would have to unlearn. Go now and deny that life is long.

38. But when you come to our own school too, I will show you many things that should be given to the axe. At a great expense of time, at great trouble to others' ears, this praise is bought: 'O man of letters!' Let us be content with this more rustic title: 'O good man!'

39. Is it so? Shall I unroll the annals of all the nations and ask who first wrote poems? Shall I, since I have no calendar, compute how much time lies between Orpheus and Homer? And shall I review the trifles of Aristarchus, with which he pricked the poems of others, and waste my years on syllables? Shall I so stick fast in the dust of geometry? Has that saving precept so slipped from me, 'Spare your time'? Shall I know these things? And what shall I not know?

40. The grammarian Apion, who went about all Greece in the days of Gaius Caesar and was adopted into the name of Homer by all the cities, used to say that Homer, when he had finished both his works, the Iliad and the Odyssey, added a beginning to his poem, in which he embraced the whole Trojan war. As proof of this argument he alleged that Homer had set in his first verse two letters by design, containing the number of his books.

41. Such things must he know who wishes to know many things, not to consider how much time bad health takes from you, how much public business, how much private business, how much daily business, how much sleep. Measure your life; it does not hold so many things.

42. I speak of the liberal studies; how much of the superfluous, how much departing from use, have the philosophers! They too have come down to the distinctions of syllables and the properties of conjunctions and prepositions, and have envied the grammarians, envied the geometers. Whatever was superfluous in those men's arts they have transferred into their own. So it has come about that they know how to speak more carefully than to live.

43. Hear how much harm too great subtlety does, and how hostile it is to truth. Protagoras says that on every matter one can argue on either side with equal force, and on this very point, whether every matter is debatable on either side. Nausiphanes says that of the things which seem to be, nothing is any more than it is not.

44. Parmenides says that of the things which seem, nothing exists except the universe. Zeno of Elea has dismissed all difficulties into one; for he says that nothing exists. About much the same lines go the Pyrrhonians and the Megarians and the Eretrians and the Academics, who have brought in a new knowledge: that we know nothing.

45. Cast all these into that superfluous herd of liberal studies; the one set hand me a knowledge that will not profit me, the other snatch away the hope of all knowledge. It is better to know superfluous things than nothing. The one set do not carry a light before me, by which my gaze may be directed toward the truth; the other dig out my eyes. If I believe Protagoras, there is nothing in the nature of things but the doubtful; if Nausiphanes, this one thing is certain, that nothing is certain; if Parmenides, there is nothing except the one; if Zeno, not even the one.

46. What, then, are we? What are these things which surround us, feed us, sustain us? The whole nature of things is a shadow, either empty or deceptive. I could not easily say with which I am more angry, those who wished us to know nothing, or those who did not leave us even this, to know nothing. Farewell.

1. That part of philosophy which gives to each person his own precepts, and does not shape man in the general, but counsels the husband how to bear himself toward his wife, the father how to rear his children, the master how to govern his slaves, some have accepted alone, leaving the rest as though wandering outside our advantage, as if anyone could give counsel about a part who had not first embraced the sum of the whole of life.

2. But Ariston the Stoic, on the contrary, holds this part to be trifling, and one that does not sink right down into the breast, having in it nothing but old wives' counsels, and says that the greatest profit comes from the very decrees of philosophy and from the definition of the highest good; "when a man has understood and learned this well, he prescribes for himself what is to be done in each particular case."

3. As one who learns to throw the javelin aims at a fixed mark and trains his hand to direct what he is to hurl, and when by training and practice he has gained this power, uses it for whatever he wishes, for he has learned to strike not this or that, but whatever he wishes: so he who has equipped himself for the whole of life does not need to be admonished piecemeal, being taught for the whole; for he has learned not how he should live with a wife or with a son, but how he should live well. And in this is included how he should live with wife and children.

4. Cleanthes judges this part useful indeed, but weak unless it flows from the whole, unless one has learned the very decrees and chief points of philosophy. This topic, then, is divided into two questions: whether it is useful or useless, and whether it alone can make a man good, that is, whether it is superfluous, or makes all the rest superfluous.

5. Those who wish this part to seem superfluous say this: "If anything set before the eyes delays the sight, it must be removed. While that thing is in the way, he who gives the precept, 'You shall walk so, you shall stretch out your hand thus,' wastes his labour. In the same way, when something blinds the mind and hinders it from discerning the order of duties, he who gives the precept, 'You shall live thus with your father, thus with your wife,' does nothing. For precepts will be of no profit so long as error is poured over the mind; if that is dispelled, it will appear what is owed to each duty. Otherwise you teach him what a healthy man should do, but you do not make him healthy.

6. You show the poor man how to act the rich man; how can this be done while his poverty remains? You show the hungry man what to do as though he were full; rather, pluck out the hunger fixed in his marrow. The same I say to you of all the vices: they themselves must be removed, and you must not prescribe what cannot be done while they remain. Unless you drive out the false opinions by which we labour, neither will the greedy man heed how money is to be used, nor the timid how to despise dangers.

7. You must bring it about that he knows money is neither good nor evil; show him the most wretched of the rich. You must bring it about that he knows that whatever we have publicly dreaded is not so much to be feared as rumour spreads abroad; that no one feels pain for long, and that it is short if great, light if long; that against pain a remedy is to be sought in firmness of mind, which makes lighter for itself whatever it has borne stubbornly. The best feature of pain's nature is that one which is prolonged cannot be great, and one which is great cannot be prolonged; that all things must be received bravely which the necessity of the universe lays upon us.

8. When by these decrees you have brought him into the sight of his own condition, and he has learned that the happy life is not the one that is according to pleasure, but the one that is according to nature; when he has loved virtue as the one good of man and shunned baseness as its only evil, and has known that the rest, riches, offices, good health, strength, dominion, are things in the middle, to be reckoned neither among goods nor among evils: then he will not need a monitor for each thing, to say, 'Walk thus, dine thus; this becomes a man, this a woman; this a married man, this an unmarried.'

9. For those who give such counsels most diligently cannot themselves do the things.
